newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya business says gov't IMF reaction "nonsense".
newsitem.headline: Kenya business says gov't IMF reaction "nonsense".

text.p: Kenyan executives and industrial analysts on Tuesday rejected as nonsense a cabinet statement that called for investor calm and declared that Kenyans should become self-reliant after the IMF cancelled a key aid package.
"That's nonsense. Kenya cannot survive without (Western) aid," said a leading Nairobi-based investment analyst.
A high-ranking corporate executive said the country should brace itself for tougher times to come.
"The cabinet is saying that Kenya can manage on its own. That is very disappointing. Kenyans must prepare for severe hardships in the next year period," he said.
The government of President Daniel arap Moi on Monday urged investors to remain calm, saying Kenyan citizens should build the economy from their own meagre resources.
"The cabinet wishes to assure Kenyans and investors in general that the situation is under control," said a statement broadcast on state television and radio.
"Kenyans are urged to continue building the economy based on their own resources so that the development of the country remains firmly in their hands."

The government gave no specific proposals on future management, but in an apparent appeal to bilateral donors not to follow the lead set by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), it said it welcomed support from development partners.

The IMF last Thursday suspended a $205 million three-year loan citing concerns over corruption, citing a scandal involving Goldenberg International to show how authorities were reticent in cracking down on corruption.
Goldenberg was paid about $100 million by the government in 1992 under a compensation scheme for gold and diamond exports. Kenya produces little gold and no diamonds.
The IMF decision severely rattled foreign exchange and equity markets. On Monday, the shilling slid with high dollar demand, easing to close at 63, 3.25 percent on Friday's close.
The World Bank has said it was studying the situation but other bilateral donors have yet to make their positions clear.
The Kenya Association of Manufacturers (KAM) and political and business leaders expressed their disappointment that the cabinet had not indicated how it would fight endemic corruption.
"Kenya has a lot of resources but if it wasn't for corruption we wouldn't need foreign aid," said world renowned palaeontologist and opposition politician Richard Leakey.
"Why are we crying about the IMF when every Kenyan has been paying taxes," Leakey said. "Because the government does not collect and what it does collect it squanders."

KAM Chairman Manu Chandaria told Reuters there were obviously difficult times ahead and urged the government to return to the negotiating table with the IMF as soon as possible to save the economy from any further battering.

"Investor confidence is not just in the hands of government. There are many forces that influence investment and the Kenyan government must be seen to take steps that will help streamline what was derailed last week," said Chandaria.
Chandaria added that Kenya needed foreign funds to develop the energy sector as well as dilapidated infrastructure and these would be deeply undermined without Western donor help.
"The amount of money that is lost through corruption is gravely high. We need the government to stop corruption and harness all available resources."

Moi, 73, and his ruling KANU party are widely expected to extend an 19-year regime in elections that must be held by the end of this year. They face an opposition that has found a fragile cohesion in demands for constitutional reforms.
